mainTopic: Found wine jugs; keeping trees and threshing floors away from a city and a neighbor's fields, and who pays when a tree is cut down.
overview: The עמוד begins by finishing the law of wine jugs found on the road. Large jugs are assumed to be Jewish because most wine pourers are Jews. Small jugs are assumed to be from travelers, unless large jugs are found with them. Then a new משנה says a tree must be kept 25 אמות from a city, or 50 for a חרוב or שקמה. It also says the tree is always cut down, and its owner is paid only if the tree clearly came first. עולא explains that the rule protects the city's beauty, and the גמרא shows this reason is needed both for רבי אלעזר and for the רבנן. The גמרא then compares the payment rules with the case of a tree near a neighbor's בור, using רב כהנא's saying that a pot shared by partners is neither hot nor cold. A second משנה requires a permanent גורן to be fifty אמות from a city. אביי and רב אשי explain its last line differently, and a ברייתא supports רב אשי. The עמוד ends as the גמרא begins to explain why a גורן must be kept away from a plowed field; the answer continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: Most wine pourers are Jews
steps.stepSummary: The end of an earlier reason: the people who pour wine are mostly Jews, so found wine jugs can be treated as Jewish wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Most] of the wine pourers are Jews.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a sentence from the discussion before this one. It explains why found wine jugs are assumed to belong to Jews.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling depends on who usually handles wine jugs. Since most of the people who pour wine into jugs are Jews, we follow the majority. That means the wine is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Wine pourers, the people who pour wine from barrels into jugs

phrases.english: that the wine pourers are Jews.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a reason that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Found wine jugs are assumed to be Jewish, because most wine pourers are Jews.

steps.title: Only large jugs are assumed to be Jewish
steps.stepSummary: The rule only covers large jugs. Small jugs are assumed to have fallen from travelers.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only to large jugs. But small jugs, say they fell from travelers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the rule it just gave. Only large jugs are treated as Jewish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Large jugs come from the wine pourers, and most of them are Jews. Small jugs are the kind travelers carry, and travelers are a different group. So small jugs do not follow the wine pourers' majority, and they are forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Travelers, people passing along the road

phrases.english: And this applies only to large ones,
but small ones —
say that they fell from travelers.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the majority rule from Step 1 to large jugs only.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Small jugs found alone are assumed to belong to travelers, so they are not assumed to be Jewish.

steps.title: Small jugs found together with large ones
steps.stepSummary: If large jugs are found together with the small ones, all of them are assumed to be Jewish. The small ones were just used to balance the load.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if there are large jugs with them, say the small ones were placed there to balance the load.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more case: small jugs found together with large jugs. In that case the small jugs follow the large ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Travelers don't usually carry large jugs. So if large jugs are there, the whole load came from the Jewish wine pourers. The small jugs were put on the animal to even out the weight.

keyTerms.meaning: Balancing the load on an animal

steps.whatToRemember: Large jugs are Jewish (most pourers are Jews). Small jugs alone are forbidden (travelers). Small jugs found with large ones are Jewish (they balanced the load).

phrases.english: And if there are large ones together with them —
say they were placed there to balance the load.
phrases.notes: Picture a donkey carrying big jugs, with small jugs added to even out the weight on each side.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a case to Step 2: small jugs found together with large ones.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Small jugs found with large jugs are assumed to be part of the same Jewish load.

steps.title: How far a tree must be kept from a city
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: a tree must be kept 25 אמות from a city, and a חרוב or שקמה must be kept 50 אמות. אבא שאול says every אילן סרק needs 50.
steps.simpleTranslation: One must keep a tree twenty-five אמות away from the city. A carob or sycamore must be kept fifty אמות away. אבא שאול says: every non-fruit tree must be kept fifty אמות away.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sets how far a tree must be from a city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The basic distance is 25 אמות. The חרוב and the שקמה need 50 because they are large trees with many branches. אבא שאול extends the 50-אמה rule to every tree that does not bear fruit.

keyTerms.meaning: A tree that does not bear fruit

phrases.english: MISHNA: One must keep a tree away
twenty-five cubits from the city,
and a carob or a sycamore — fifty cubits.
Abba Shaul says:
every non-fruit tree — fifty cubits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tree must be 25 אמות from a city; a חרוב or שקמה must be 50. אבא שאול says every אילן סרק must be 50.

steps.title: Who pays when the tree is cut down
steps.stepSummary: The tree is always cut down. Whether the owner is paid depends on which came first, the city or the tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the city came first, he cuts it down and gets no money. If the tree came first, he cuts it down and gets paid. If it is unclear which came first, he cuts it down and gets no money.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה goes on to explain payment when a tree is too close to a city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In every case the tree is cut down. If the tree was there first, its owner did nothing wrong, so the city pays him. If the city was first, or if no one knows which was first, the owner gets nothing.
steps.confusionAlert: Even when the tree was there first, it is still cut down. The only thing that changes is whether the owner gets paid.

phrases.english: And if the city came first —
he cuts it down, and is not given money;
and if the tree came first —
he cuts it down, and is given money;

phrases.aramaic: סָפֵק זֶה קָדַם וְסָפֵק זֶה קָדַם –
phrases.english: if it is uncertain whether this one or that one came first —
he cuts it down, and is not given money.
phrases.notes: The city is the one who would pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה from Step 4 with the rules of payment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The tree is always cut down. The owner is paid only if the tree clearly came first.

steps.title: Why must a tree be kept away from a city?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the משנה's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by asking why trees must be kept away from a city. This sets up עולא's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave distances but no reason. Knowing the reason matters, because it decides what the rule is protecting.

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the משנה in Step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a tree must be kept away from a city.

steps.title: עולא: for the beauty of the city
steps.stepSummary: עולא answers that trees are kept away to protect the city's beauty.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: because of the beauty of the city.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא gives the reason for the משנה's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is about how the city looks, not about damage. A clear open area around the city keeps it attractive.

phrases.english: Ulla said:
Because of the beauty of the city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The trees are kept away for the beauty of the city.

steps.title: Why not use the rule about the city's open area?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: why do we need עולא's reason, when we already have the rule that a שדה may not be made into a מגרש, or a מגרש into a שדה?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him get it from the rule that one may not make a field into an open area, nor an open area into a field!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges עולא's reason. It points to another rule that should already forbid planting trees near the city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The open strip around a city, the מגרש, has to stay open. Planting trees there would turn it into a שדה, which is already forbidden. So it seems עולא's reason of beauty is not needed.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him get it from (a different source)
The open area around a city

phrases.english: But let him derive it
from the rule that one may not make a field into an open area,
phrases.notes: This is the open area around the cities in במדבר 35. Planting trees there would turn it into a field.

phrases.english: nor an open area into a field!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתִיפּוֹק לֵיהּ דְּאֵין עוֹשִׂין שָׂדֶה מִגְרָשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether עולא's reason in Step 7 is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: עולא's reason of the city's beauty
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule against turning a מגרש into a שדה already forbids planting trees near the city, so the beauty reason seems unnecessary.

steps.title: The beauty reason is needed for רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that עולא's reason is needed for רבי אלעזר. He allows changing a שדה into a מגרש and back, but still agrees that trees are kept away for the city's beauty.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for רבי אלעזר, who said: one may make a field into an open area and an open area into a field. Here, because of the beauty of the city, we do not do it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends עולא's reason. It shows a view under which the מגרש rule would not be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר allows switching land between שדה and מגרש, so that rule cannot forbid the trees in his view. Only עולא's reason, the beauty of the city, explains the משנה according to him. That is why עולא's reason is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed (only) for this case

steps.whatToRemember: Trees are kept away from a city for its beauty (עולא). This reason is needed because רבי אלעזר allows turning a שדה into a מגרש and back.

phrases.english: It is needed
according to Rabbi Elazar, who said:
one may make a field into an open area and an open area into a field;

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא מִשּׁוּם נוֹיֵי הָעִיר לָא עָבְדִינַן.
phrases.english: here, because of the beauty of the city, we do not do it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the need for the reason to one opinion, רבי אלעזר's
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule that a מגרש may not become a שדה already explains the משנה, so עולא's reason adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי אלעזר, who allows the change, only the city's beauty explains why the trees are kept away.

steps.title: Even the רבנן need the city's beauty reason
steps.stepSummary: Even according to the רבנן, the rule against turning a שדה into a מגרש only covers seeds. Trees would normally be allowed, so עולא's beauty reason is needed to forbid them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even for the רבנן, who say you may not turn a field into an open area or an open area into a field, that rule is only about seeds. Trees may be planted there. But here, near the city, trees are not allowed because of the city's beauty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer to the question in Step 8. It shows that עולא's reason is needed even according to the רבנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 9 the answer was that עולא is needed for רבי אלעזר. Now the גמרא says he is needed for the רבנן too. Their rule only stops planting seeds in a מגרש. Without עולא's reason, trees would be allowed, so the beauty reason is what keeps trees away from the city.

phrases.english: And also according to the Rabbis, who say:
one may not make a field into an open area
nor an open area into a field
this applies only to seeds,
phrases.notes: He means: sowing seeds in the open area is what turns it into a field.

phrases.english: but trees, we do plant there;
and here, because of the city's beauty, we do not.

steps.whatToRemember: עולא's reason (the city's beauty) is needed according to everyone. For רבי אלעזר it is needed because he allows changing a field into an open area. For the רבנן it is needed because their rule only covers seeds, not trees.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to Step 8, adding to Step 9's answer about רבי אלעזר.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of the other rule (it covers seeds only)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule against turning a field into an open area already keeps trees away, so עולא's reason adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: That rule only forbids seeds. Trees are kept away only because of the city's beauty.

steps.title: How do we know seeds and trees are different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source showing that seeds and trees are treated differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do you know that seeds and trees are different?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for proof of the claim it just made in Step 10. This sets up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10's answer depends on the idea that planting trees does not turn an open area into a field, while sowing seeds does. The גמרא wants a source for this difference before relying on it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do you say this? (a request for a source)

phrases.english: And from where do you say
that there is a difference between seeds and trees?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the seeds/trees difference used in Step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that trees do not change the character of an area the way seeds do.

steps.title: Proof from a large enclosure on שבת
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא about carrying on שבת shows that sowing most of a קרפף makes it like a garden, but planting trees in most of it leaves it like a courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: a large enclosure, bigger than two בית סאה, that was fenced in for living. If most of it was sown with seeds, it is like a garden, and carrying there is forbidden. If most of it was planted with trees, it is like a courtyard, and carrying there is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that seeds and trees are treated differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A big enclosure counts as a living area only if it is used for living. Sowing seeds turns it into a garden, which is not a living area, so carrying is forbidden. Planting trees does not change it, and it stays like a courtyard. This proves that trees do not change what kind of place an area is, but seeds do.

keyTerms.meaning: A fenced-in enclosure, usually behind houses
An area big enough to sow two סאה of seed
Fenced in for the purpose of living there

phrases.english: As it was taught in a ברייתא:
an enclosure bigger than two בית סאה
that was fenced in for living;
if most of it was sown with seeds,
it is like a garden, and carrying there is forbidden;
if most of it was planted with trees,
it is like a courtyard, and carrying there is allowed.

steps.confusionAlert: This ברייתא is about carrying on שבת, not about cities or trees near a city. The גמרא only borrows the idea that trees do not change an area's status, while seeds do.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 11's question with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: Planting trees does not change an area into a 'field' the way sowing seeds does.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא about a קרפף larger than two בית סאה that was fenced in for living.

steps.title: Back to the משנה: if the city came first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's next line: if the city came first, the tree is cut down and the owner is not paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if the city came first, he cuts down the tree and is not paid, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and quotes a new line from it. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic changes here. The גמרא moves from the reason for keeping trees away to the question of payment. It quotes the case where the city came first, in which the tree owner gets nothing.

phrases.english: And if the city came first,
he cuts it down and is not paid, etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the seeds/trees discussion and returns to the משנה's ruling on payment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the city was there before the tree, the tree is cut down with no payment to its owner.

steps.title: Why is the cistern case different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why, near a neighbor's בור, the tree owner is paid when he cuts down his tree, but near a city that came first he is not paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about a cistern, where the משנה teaches that he cuts down the tree and is paid, and what is different here, where it teaches that he cuts it down and is not paid?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out what looks like a contradiction between two משניות about cutting down trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases a tree hurts something that was there first and must be cut down. Yet another משנה says the tree owner is paid in the case of a בור, while our משנה says he is not paid when the city came first. The גמרא wants to know why the two cases have different results.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? (asking why two cases are treated differently)
A cistern, a pit for collecting water

phrases.english: What is different about a cistern,
phrases.notes: This is a different משנה, about a tree planted near a neighbor's cistern that was there first.

phrases.english: where it teaches: he cuts it down and is paid;
and what is different here,
where it teaches: he cuts it down and is not paid?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה's ruling quoted in Step 13 by comparing it to the cistern משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that the tree owner is not paid when the city came first.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the very similar case of a tree near a neighbor's earlier cistern, the tree owner is paid. Why should the city case be different?

steps.title: A pot shared by partners is neither hot nor cold
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא answers the question from Step 14 with a well-known saying about partners.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: A pot owned by partners is neither hot nor cold.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא answers why the tree owner near a city is not paid. He uses a popular saying: when many people share something, nobody takes care of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With one neighbor near a בור, there is a clear person who pays. A city is made of many people, and each one leaves the job to the others, so no one person would ever arrange the payment. That is why the משנה does not require the city to pay.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
A pot belonging to partners
is neither hot nor cold.
phrases.notes: Each partner expects another one to heat the pot, so it never really gets heated. Nobody takes charge of something that everyone owns.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא: קִידְרָא דְּבֵי שׁוּתָּפֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasoning: a group of shared owners will not get organized to pay.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The city should pay just like a neighbor with a בור does.
steps.terutzMaskana: A city is many owners, and nobody takes charge of paying, so the משנה does not require payment.

steps.title: The question itself was weak
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why there was a question at all, since harm to the public may simply be different from harm to one person.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the difficulty? Maybe damage to the public is different from damage to an individual!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the question from Step 14, not on רב כהנא's saying. It suggests there was never a real problem to begin with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is an easy reason the two cases differ. Someone whose tree harms the whole public (רבים) may have to cut it down for free, while someone whose tree harms one person (יחיד) is paid. Once the question falls away, רב כהנא's answer is not needed here, which sets up the next move: putting his saying somewhere else.

keyTerms.meaning: and what is the difficulty? (the question was never a real problem)

phrases.english: And what is the difficulty?
Perhaps damage to the public is different
from damage to an individual!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 14 another way, so the answer in Step 15 no longer belongs there.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the question from Step 14, and with it the placement of רב כהנא's answer there.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The question ignored a simple difference: harm to the public versus harm to one person.

steps.title: Moving רב כהנא's saying to the next clause
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רב כהנא's saying was really said about the next clause of the משנה: if the tree came first, it is cut down and the city pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if רב כהנא's saying was stated, it was stated about the last clause: if the tree came first, he cuts it down and is paid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves רב כהנא's saying to a new place in the משנה. It quotes that clause to set up a new question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the tree was there before the city, so the city must pay (נותן דמים) for the tree. The next step will ask about the timing of that payment.

keyTerms.meaning: about the last clause (of the משנה)

phrases.english: Rather, if Rav Kahana's statement was said,
it was said about the last clause:
If the tree came first,
he cuts it down and money is given.
phrases.notes: The city is the one paying the tree owner here.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִי אִיתְּמַר דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא, אַסֵּיפָא אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After Step 16 removed the original setting, this gives רב כהנא's saying a new setting.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the tree came before the city, it is cut down and the city pays its value.

steps.title: Why not pay first and cut later?
steps.stepSummary: The tree owner should be able to say: pay me first, then I will cut.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say to them: Give me the money first, and then I will cut it down!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the tree is cut before the owner gets paid. It seems fair for him to demand payment first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says 'cuts and pays,' which sounds like the cutting comes first. The question is why the owner cannot hold onto his tree until the city pays him.

keyTerms.meaning: and let him say to them

phrases.english: And let him say to them:
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the people of the city.

phrases.english: Give me the money first,
and then I will cut it down!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵימָא לְהוּ: הַבוּ לִי בְּרֵישָׁא דְּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the order of 'cut, then pay' in the clause quoted in Step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The order in the משנה: the tree is cut before payment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone owed money for his property should be able to demand payment before he gives up the property.

steps.title: Partners never get organized, so the cutting comes first
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא's saying is used again: a group of partners would never pay quickly, so the tree is cut first.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: A pot of partners is neither hot nor cold.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רב כהנא's saying, now as the answer in its new place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner could wait until the city collected the money, the tree might stand for a very long time, because nobody in a group takes charge. So the city cuts the tree right away and pays afterward, unlike a single person who could be told to pay first.

keyTerms.meaning: partners (here, the people of the city)

steps.whatToRemember: רב כהנא's saying does not explain why the city doesn't pay. It explains why, when the city does pay, it may cut the tree first and pay afterward.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
A pot belonging to partners
is neither hot nor cold.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא: קִידְרָא דְּבֵי שׁוּתָּפֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 18 by placing רב כהנא's saying here.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical reasoning about how groups behave.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner may demand payment before cutting.
steps.terutzMaskana: A city would delay payment for a long time, so the tree is cut first and paid for later.

steps.title: When no one knows which came first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה: if it is unknown whether the tree or the city came first, the tree is cut down and no money is paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is unknown whether this came first or that came first, he cuts it down and is not paid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to quote the next case in the משנה, a case of doubt (ספק). It is setting up a question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the tree must still be cut for the city's sake. Because nobody can show the tree came first, the owner gets no money.

phrases.aramaic: סָפֵק זֶה קָדַם וְסָפֵק זֶה קָדַם –
phrases.english: If it is uncertain whether this one came first or that one came first,
phrases.notes: 'This one' and 'that one' mean the tree and the city.

phrases.english: he cuts it down and money is not given.

steps.triggerLanguage: סָפֵק זֶה קָדַם וְסָפֵק זֶה קָדַם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the משנה (Step 5) and quotes its last clause, the case of doubt, to set up a new question.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a doubt next to a city, the tree is cut down without payment.

steps.title: Why is a doubt near a city different from a doubt near a בור?
steps.stepSummary: Next to a בור, a doubt means the tree is not cut at all. So why is it cut here?
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from a בור, where you said he does not cut it down?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rule just quoted by comparing it to the rule about a neighbor's בור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a tree near a neighbor's בור, the משנה later rules that in a doubt the tree stays. Here, in the same kind of doubt, the tree is cut down. The גמרא wants to know what makes the two cases different.

keyTerms.meaning: he shall not cut it down

phrases.english: What is different from a cistern,
where you said: He does not cut it down?
phrases.notes: This points to the rule in a different משנה, a little later in the פרק: a tree near a neighbor's בור when no one knows which came first.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא מִבּוֹר, דְּאָמְרַתְּ: לֹא יָקוֹץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the doubt ruling quoted in Step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that in a doubt next to a city, the tree is cut down.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the same kind of doubt next to a בור, the tree is left standing, so the two rulings seem to contradict each other.

steps.title: Why a doubtful tree is cut near a city but not near a pit
steps.stepSummary: Near a בור, even a tree that surely came first is not cut, so a doubt leaves it standing. Near a city, every tree is cut anyway, so a doubt means it is still cut. The doubt only matters for money, and the owner must bring proof to get paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: There (by the בור), where even in a sure case the tree would not be cut, in a doubt we also don't tell him 'cut.' Here (by the city), where even in a sure case the tree would be cut, in a doubt we also tell him 'cut.' And if he wants money, we tell him: bring proof and take it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 21: why is the tree cut here when the case is in doubt, while next to a בור it is not?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Next to a בור, the doubt is about whether the tree must be cut at all. If it came first, it stays, so in a doubt we leave it. Next to a city, the tree is cut no matter what. The only doubt is whether the city pays, and someone who wants money from another must bring proof.

keyTerms.meaning: it stands to be cut down
money, the value of the tree
bring proof and take your money

steps.whatToRemember: Near a city, the tree is cut down in every case, and the doubt only decides whether money is paid. Without proof, the owner gets nothing.
steps.confusionAlert: The doubt does not decide whether the tree is cut. It is cut anyway. The doubt only decides whether the owner gets paid.

phrases.english: There, where in a sure case it does not stand to be cut,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the tree next to a בור from Step 21, where a tree that came first is not cut.

phrases.english: in its case of doubt, too, we do not tell him "Cut";
here, where in a sure case it does stand to be cut,
in its case of doubt, too, we tell him "Cut."
And if he complains because of the money,
we tell him: Bring proof and take it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 21
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Doubt should work the same way near a city as near a בור, so the tree should stay.
steps.terutzMaskana: Near a city the tree is cut in every case. The doubt only touches the payment, and that needs proof.

steps.title: New משנה: how far to keep a threshing floor
steps.stepSummary: A permanent גורן must be fifty אמות from the city. One may not set up a permanent גורן on his own land unless he has fifty אמות of space in every direction. He must also keep it far enough from a neighbor's plants and plowed field that it does no damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: A permanent גורן is kept fifty אמות away from the city. A person may not make a permanent גורן on his own land unless he has fifty אמות in every direction. He must keep it away from his neighbor's plants and plowed field, enough that it causes no damage.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It sets distance rules for a threshing floor, because the chaff blown from it can harm people and plants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives a fixed number, fifty אמות, for distance from a city and from the edges of one's own land. For a neighbor's plants and field, it gives no number and only says 'enough not to damage.' This difference is what the גמרא will ask about next.

phrases.english: MISHNA: We distance a permanent threshing floor
fifty cubits from the city.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא יַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם גּוֹרֶן קָבוּעַ בְּתוֹךְ שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: A person should not make a permanent threshing floor within his own property,
unless he has
fifty cubits in every direction;
and he distances it from his fellow's plantings and from his plowed field,
enough so that it does not cause damage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A permanent גורן needs fifty אמות from the city and from the edges of one's own land, and enough distance from a neighbor's plants and field to do no damage.

steps.title: Why a fixed number first and only 'enough' later?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the first part of the משנה gives fifty אמות while the last part only says 'enough not to damage.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about the first part, and what is different about the last part?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the two parts of the משנה do not seem to match. It asks why one part has a set number and the other does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If chaff from a גורן reaches fifty אמות, the same distance should apply to a neighbor's plants. The משנה switches to a general 'enough not to damage,' so the גמרא wants to know what changed.

keyTerms.meaning: the first part of the משנה
the last part of the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: What is different about the first clause,
and what is different about the latter clause?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא רֵישָׁא וּמַאי שְׁנָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the משנה in Step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: The two parts of the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same גורן should need the same distance, so why does one part give fifty אמות and the other only 'enough'?

steps.title: אביי: the last part is about a non-permanent threshing floor
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the last part of the משנה is about a גורן that is not permanent, which needs less distance.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: in the last part, we have moved on to a threshing floor that is not permanent.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question by saying the two parts of the משנה are talking about two different kinds of גורן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A permanent גורן makes a lot of chaff, so it needs a fixed fifty אמות. A non-permanent one makes less chaff, so it only needs to be far enough not to cause damage.

keyTerms.meaning: we have come to, we are now talking about
a threshing floor that is not permanent

phrases.english: Abaye said:
In the latter clause, we have come to a threshing floor that is not permanent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי סֵיפָא אֲתָאן לְגוֹרֶן שֶׁאֵינוֹ קָבוּעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case: each clause is about a different kind of גורן
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both parts are about the same permanent גורן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first part is about a permanent גורן, and the last part is about a non-permanent one.

steps.title: What counts as a non-permanent threshing floor?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how a non-permanent גורן is defined.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case of a threshing floor that is not permanent?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that אביי has brought in a 'non-permanent' גורן, the גמרא asks what exactly that means. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה never defines 'permanent' or 'non-permanent.' The גמרא needs a clear definition to know which distance rule applies.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? how does it look?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances of a threshing floor that is not permanent?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a definition of the term אביי used in Step 25
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The definition of a non-permanent גורן

steps.title: Definition: grain not winnowed with a shovel
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא says a non-permanent גורן is any one where the grain is not winnowed with a רחת (shovel).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: any threshing floor where he does not winnow with a shovel.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא answers the question with a clear definition of a non-permanent גורן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Throwing grain into the wind with a shovel scatters chaff far, which is what a big, permanent גורן does. A small amount of grain winnowed without a shovel spreads less chaff. So it only needs enough distance not to cause damage.

keyTerms.meaning: winnows, tosses grain in the wind to blow away the chaff

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, a permanent גורן needs a fixed fifty אמות. A non-permanent גורן, where the grain is not winnowed with a רחת, only needs to be far enough not to cause damage. (רב אשי reads the משנה differently in the next step.)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
Any one where he does not winnow with a winnowing shovel.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא כׇּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ זוֹרֶה בְּרַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 26
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A non-permanent גורן is one where the grain is not winnowed with a רחת.

steps.title: רב אשי: 'Enough not to damage' is the reason for fifty אמות
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers the contradiction in the משנה differently from אביי. The phrase 'so that it does not damage' explains why there are fifty אמות. It is not a second, smaller measurement.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: The משנה is giving a reason. Why must a permanent threshing floor be kept fifty אמות from the city? So that it does not cause damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי offers a second answer to the question from Step 24. He says the end of the משנה is not giving a new distance. It is explaining the first one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי said the two parts of the משנה deal with two kinds of גורן. רב אשי says there is only one rule, fifty אמות, and 'so that it does not damage' is simply the reason for it. That means a neighbor's crops also get the full fifty אמות.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is saying what the reason is.' The words explain a rule; they do not add a new one.
So that it does not cause damage

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the coming test. If a source requires fifty אמות from crops 'so that it does not damage,' it supports רב אשי over אביי.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It is stating a reason —
phrases.notes: The last words of the משנה explain the fifty אמות. They are not a new, smaller distance.

phrases.english: what is the reason one must distance a permanent threshing floor
fifty cubits from the city?
So that it does not cause damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: מַה טַּעַם קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the question in Step 24, in place of אביי's answer in Step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the wording: the phrase is a reason, not a separate measurement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The end of the משנה seemed to set a smaller distance than the fifty אמות at the beginning.
steps.terutzMaskana: There is one distance, fifty אמות. 'So that it does not damage' is its reason.

steps.title: A ברייתא requires fifty אמות from a neighbor's crops
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that requires fifty אמות from a neighbor's gourds, cucumbers, plantings and plowed field, 'so that it does not damage.' This fits רב אשי but is hard for אביי.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged from a ברייתא: A permanent threshing floor must be kept fifty אמות from the city. Just as it is kept fifty אמות from the city, it must also be kept fifty אמות from a neighbor's gourds, cucumbers, plantings and plowed field, so that it does not cause damage. This works well for רב אשי, but it is difficult for אביי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to test the two answers. It finds that the ברייתא matches רב אשי and challenges אביי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא puts 'fifty אמות' and 'so that it does not damage' together, for the neighbor's crops too. That is exactly how רב אשי reads the משנה. אביי said the crops case needs less than fifty אמות, so the ברייתא contradicts him.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Granted... it works out well': this view has no problem

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
One must distance a permanent threshing floor from the city
fifty cubits.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְשֵׁם שֶׁמַּרְחִיקִין מִן הָעִיר חֲמִשִּׁים אַמָּה,
phrases.english: And just as one distances it fifty cubits from the city,
so too one distances it from the gourds and cucumbers
and plantings and plowed field of his fellow —
fifty cubits, so that it does not cause damage.
Granted, according to Rav Ashi it works out well,
but according to Abaye it is difficult!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: מַרְחִיקִין גּוֹרֶן קָבוּעַ מִן הָעִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the two answers (אביי in Step 25 and רב אשי in Step 28) against a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's answer that the crops case is about a non-permanent גורן needing a smaller distance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא requires the same fifty אמות from crops and links it to 'so that it does not damage.' So that phrase means fifty אמות, not less.

steps.title: The גמרא agrees: אביי's answer remains difficult
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says one word, 'קשיא.' It agrees the ברייתא is a real difficulty for אביי and gives no answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is indeed difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits it has no answer for אביי here. The question is left standing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not try to defend אביי. The ברייתא matches רב אשי's reading, so his view is left as the stronger one.
steps.confusionAlert: 'קשיא' is not the same as 'תיובתא' (a full refutation). The גמרא leaves a hard question on אביי, but it does not declare his view completely rejected.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא supports רב אשי: a permanent גורן needs fifty אמות from a neighbor's crops and plowed field too. 'So that it does not damage' is the reason, not a smaller distance.

phrases.english: It is difficult.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of Step 29 without answering it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: אביי's answer is left with an unanswered difficulty, and רב אשי's reading stands.

steps.title: Why must a גורן be kept away from a plowed field?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא understands why cucumbers and gourds are hurt: the chaff gets into them and dries them out. But a plowed field has nothing growing in it, so why does it need distance?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for his cucumbers and gourds, because the chaff flies into their heart and dries them out. But why from his plowed field?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now asks about the ברייתא itself. It wants to know what damage the גורן could do to an empty plowed field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With growing plants, the damage is clear: chaff gets inside and dries them out. A plowed field has no plants yet, so the reason for the distance there is not obvious. The גמרא asks what harm it suffers.

keyTerms.meaning: Chaff, the dust that flies off the threshing floor

phrases.english: Granted, from his cucumbers and gourds —
because the chaff goes and enters into its heart
and dries it out;
but from his plowed field — why?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from which view the ברייתא supports to understanding one item listed in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What damage a threshing floor causes to a plowed field with no crops in it

steps.title: רבי אבא בר זבדא begins to explain the plowed field
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר זבדא (some say רבי אבא בר זוטרא) begins to answer with 'because...'. His explanation continues in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר זבדא said, and some say it was רבי אבא בר זוטרא: Because...
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא starts to answer the question about the plowed field. Only his first word appears here; the rest of his answer continues next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא is not sure which of two rabbis said this answer, so it names both. The word 'מפני' tells us a reason for the plowed-field damage is coming.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said,
and some say it was Rabbi Abba bar Zutra:
Because…
phrases.notes: His sentence keeps going on the next עמוד.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זַבְדָּא, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר זוּטְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of Step 31.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The answer begins here with 'because' and continues in the following text.
